<reason>B built a more testable, falsifiable case (primary balance at full employment) and used it to expose A's central weakness: when directly pressed for a threshold at which deficit reduction should bind, A explicitly declined to give one, calling any number "false precision." B correctly turned this into the closing frame ("which rule can ever say no?"), which A's closing never rebutted. B also landed the sharpest substantive rebuttal of the debate—"the stock is nothing but the accumulated flow"—directly undercutting A's productive/unproductive spending distinction, and refined it further into a financing-based ("paid for") standard that A never engaged with in later rounds. A's WWII/denominator analogy, the centerpiece of its opening, was met with three concrete disanalogies (primary surpluses from demobilization, favorable demographics, negative real rates) that A never squarely answered, instead reasserting the same growth-mechanism claim in closing while inaccurately asserting B "never rebutted" it. Both sides suffered clipped speeches (A once, B twice), a real execution cost, but the substantive content lost appears to be trailing rhetorical flourishes rather than core argument, and B's greater clipping cost is outweighed by its sharper, more adaptive engagement across rounds.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 point that "the stock IS nothing but the accumulated flow" [B2.6], paired with A's failure in Rebuttal 2/Closing to answer it or B's later threshold demand, was the most decisive exchange—it neutralized A's core stock-vs-flow distinction and exposed A's rule as one that, by its own admission, never fires.</best_rebuttal>
